New machine. Its objects are: gilisak, binirel, kebivu, nopumen, natumes, ladetes.
You have 5 tests. Make your first move.

I'll start by testing half of the objects together to narrow down where the nexioms are.

TEST: gilisak, binirel, kebivu
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have 4 tests left. Make your next move.

The first group of three did not light. If the machine lights whenever at least one nexiom is present, both nexioms must be among the other three. If it needs both nexioms present, I only know they weren't both in that first group. Testing two of the remaining three will help tell these cases apart.

TEST: nopumen, natumes
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have 3 tests left. Make your next move.

Neither test lit the machine. If one nexiom alone were enough to light it, both nexioms would have to be among nopumen, natumes and ladetes. But nopumen and natumes did not light, so only ladetes could be a nexiom, which contradicts there being two. So the machine probably needs both nexioms present at once.

Under that rule, 11 pairs are still possible:
- any pair with one of gilisak, binirel or kebivu and one of nopumen, natumes or ladetes;
- nopumen with ladetes;
- natumes with ladetes.

Testing gilisak, binirel, nopumen and ladetes splits these roughly in half: 5 pairs would light it and 6 would not.

TEST: gilisak, binirel, nopumen, ladetes
Result: the machine LIT UP. You have 2 tests left. Make your next move.

If the machine lights only when both nexioms are present, test 3 means both are among gilisak, binirel, nopumen and ladetes. With the two earlier failed tests, five pairs remain possible:
- gilisak with nopumen
- gilisak with ladetes
- binirel with nopumen
- binirel with ladetes
- nopumen with ladetes

Two yes/no tests can tell apart at most four cases, so I may have to guess at the end. Testing gilisak, binirel and nopumen splits the five pairs into two that would light it and three that would not.

TEST: gilisak, binirel, nopumen
Result: the machine LIT UP. You have 1 test left. Make your next move.

If the machine needs both nexioms at once, only two pairs still fit all four results: gilisak with nopumen, or binirel with nopumen. Testing gilisak and nopumen together separates them: it lights only if they are the pair.

This rests on the both-needed rule, which I inferred from the first two tests rather than proved. A rule like "lights when exactly one nexiom is present" would also fit the four results. One test cannot rule that out as well, so I'm spending it on the more likely rule.

TEST: gilisak, nopumen
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have used all your tests. Give your ANSWER now.

If the machine lights only when both nexioms are present, the answer is binirel and nopumen. Gilisak, binirel and nopumen lit the machine, but gilisak and nopumen alone did not, so the second nexiom must be binirel.

This is not certain. A machine that lights when exactly one nexiom is present would fit all five results with binirel and kebivu instead. Both rules point to binirel; the uncertainty is only about the second nexiom. I'm going with the both-needed rule because the first two tests suggested it.

ANSWER: nexioms = binirel, nopumen
One last question. If only binirel were on the machine, with nothing else, would it light up? End your message with one line: PROBE: yes or PROBE: no

I predict it would **not** light up. My answer rests on the rule that the machine lights only when both nexioms are on it together. With binirel alone, only one nexiom would be present.

This is not certain. My tests never ruled out the other rule I mentioned, where the machine lights when exactly one nexiom is present. Under that rule the nexioms would be binirel and kebivu, and binirel alone *would* light it. I'm staying consistent with the rule I bet on, but this prediction is only as reliable as that assumption.

PROBE: no

New machine. Its objects are: simuzul, litofen, vilator, rikoris, zovedos, fezogik.
You have 5 tests. Make your first move.

I'll start by testing half of the objects to narrow down where the nexioms are.

TEST: simuzul, litofen, vilator
Result: the machine LIT UP. You have 4 tests left. Make your next move.

The first group lit up, but I don't yet know whether the machine needs one nexiom or both. Testing the other half will help separate those possibilities.

TEST: rikoris, zovedos, fezogik
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have 3 tests left. Make your next move.

The first group lit up and the second did not. That rules out a machine that lights for exactly one nexiom, because each group would then hold one nexiom and both would have lit. The machine must light either when at least one nexiom is present or only when both are. Either way, both nexioms are among simuzul, litofen and vilator.

Testing simuzul and litofen together will help separate those cases. It lights if the machine needs only one nexiom, or if it needs both and simuzul and litofen are the pair.

TEST: simuzul, litofen
Result: the machine LIT UP. You have 2 tests left. Make your next move.

Both nexioms are among simuzul, litofen and vilator. The machine lights either when at least one nexiom is present or only when both are. That leaves four possibilities:
- If the machine needs both nexioms, the pair must be simuzul and litofen.
- If one nexiom is enough, the pair could be simuzul+litofen, simuzul+vilator or litofen+vilator.

Testing vilator alone separates these. If it does not light, the pair is simuzul and litofen under either rule. If it lights, vilator is a nexiom and one is enough. Then testing simuzul alone tells me whether the other nexiom is simuzul or litofen.

TEST: vilator
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have 1 test left. Make your next move.

Vilator alone did not light up, so vilator is not a nexiom under either rule.

- **If one nexiom is enough:** vilator is ruled out. The pair must then be the remaining two from the first group, simuzul and litofen.
- **If the machine needs both:** the test with simuzul and litofen lit up, so they are the pair.

Both rules give the same answer, so I don't need the last test.

ANSWER: nexioms = simuzul, litofen
One last question. If only litofen were on the machine, with nothing else, would it light up? End your message with one line: PROBE: yes or PROBE: no

**I can't tell from my tests whether litofen alone would light the machine.**

The tests show the nexioms are simuzul and litofen. They also show the machine lights either when at least one nexiom is present or only when both are present. Every test result fits both rules:
- **If one nexiom is enough,** litofen alone would light the machine.
- **If both are needed,** litofen alone would not.

Testing simuzul or litofen alone would have settled it, but I stopped once the pair was identified.

This answer is a guess. I'm choosing the "at least one" rule because it is the simpler, more common way a detector works.

PROBE: yes

New machine. Its objects are: lekilis, fitagak, givemak, sibebor, barini, sinise.
You have 5 tests. Make your first move.

I'll start by testing half of the objects to see how the machine responds.

TEST: lekilis, fitagak, givemak
Result: the machine LIT UP. You have 4 tests left. Make your next move.

The first group lit up, but I don't know the rule yet. It could light when any nexiom is present, only when both are, or only when exactly one is. Testing the other three objects will help tell these apart.

TEST: sibebor, barini, sinise
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have 3 tests left. Make your next move.

The second group did not light up, which rules out "exactly one nexiom present." If it were that rule, the second group would also hold exactly one nexiom and would have lit. So the rule is probably either "lights if any nexiom is present" or "lights only if both are present." Either way, both nexioms must be among lekilis, fitagak and givemak.

That leaves three possible pairs: lekilis + fitagak, lekilis + givemak, or fitagak + givemak. I'll test lekilis and fitagak together.
- **If it doesn't light:** the rule must be "both needed," and the pair isn't lekilis + fitagak. One more test settles which pair it is.
- **If it lights:** testing givemak alone tells me whether the pair is lekilis + fitagak. If it isn't, testing lekilis alone separates the other two pairs.

TEST: lekilis, fitagak
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have 2 tests left. Make your next move.

lekilis + fitagak did NOT light up, so the rule cannot be "lights if any nexiom is present." Any pair from the first group includes lekilis or fitagak, so that test would have lit. The rule must be "lights only when both nexioms are present."

That leaves two possible pairs: lekilis + givemak or fitagak + givemak. Testing lekilis and givemak together settles it.
- **If it lights:** the nexioms are lekilis and givemak.
- **If it doesn't:** the nexioms are fitagak and givemak.

I'd still have one test spare to confirm.

TEST: lekilis, givemak
Result: the machine LIT UP. You have 1 test left. Make your next move.

I need to double-check my earlier reasoning, which assumed the rule treats both nexioms the same way. It might not. Here is what the four tests show:
- **lekilis + givemak** fits a "lights only when both are present" rule. It also fits a lopsided rule where givemak lights the machine on its own.
- **fitagak + givemak** also fits that lopsided rule. lekilis + fitagak didn't light because only fitagak was there. lekilis + givemak lit because givemak was there.
- **givemak plus any of sibebor, barini or sinise** fits the same lopsided rule.
- **Every other pair** contradicts at least one result.

The key question is whether givemak alone lights the machine.
- **If it doesn't light:** every alternative is ruled out, and the nexioms are lekilis and givemak.
- **If it lights:** the lopsided explanations stay open, and I'll have to choose between them.

TEST: givemak
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have used all your tests. Give your ANSWER now.

Every result fits only one pair: **lekilis and givemak**, with the machine lighting only when both nexioms are present.
- **lekilis + givemak** lit, and every test containing both of them lit.
- **lekilis, fitagak, givemak** lit, consistent with that pair.
- **lekilis + fitagak** did not light, because givemak was missing.
- **givemak alone** did not light, because lekilis was missing.
- **sibebor, barini, sinise** did not light, because neither nexiom was there.

Every other pair contradicts at least one result:
- **givemak with fitagak, sibebor, barini or sinise:** lekilis + givemak would contain only givemak and still light, yet givemak alone did not.
- **lekilis with fitagak, sibebor, barini or sinise:** lekilis + fitagak would contain lekilis and fail, while lekilis + givemak also contains only lekilis and lit. If the pair is lekilis + fitagak itself, they were both present yet it failed, while the first group lit with the same pair.
- **Any pair from sibebor, barini and sinise:** the first group would contain no nexiom yet still lit.

ANSWER: nexioms = lekilis, givemak
One last question. If only givemak were on the machine, with nothing else, would it light up? End your message with one line: PROBE: yes or PROBE: no

No, it would not light. I tested givemak alone directly, and the machine did not light up. This fits the conclusion that it lights only when both lekilis and givemak are present.

PROBE: no

New machine. Its objects are: sudokes, gidimur, kigabe, lireru, dizabir, tefisi.
You have 5 tests. Make your first move.

I'll start by testing half of the objects to narrow things down.

TEST: sudokes, gidimur, kigabe
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have 4 tests left. Make your next move.

The first group of three didn't light the machine, but I don't yet know the rule. It might light when any nexiom is present, or only when both are. Testing the other three objects should help tell those apart. If they light up, then under either rule both nexioms are probably in that group.

TEST: lireru, dizabir, tefisi
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have 3 tests left. Make your next move.

Neither group of three lit the machine. Since both nexioms are somewhere among the six, at least one group held a nexiom. So the machine does not light whenever any nexiom is present. The most likely rule is that it lights only when both nexioms are on it. That would mean one nexiom is among sudokes, gidimur and kigabe, and the other is among lireru, dizabir and tefisi.

That leaves 9 possible pairs. Three yes/no tests give at most 8 outcomes, so I may not be able to separate every case. I'll test two objects from each group, which splits the 9 pairs into 4 that would light and 5 that would not.

TEST: sudokes, gidimur, lireru, dizabir
Result: the machine LIT UP. You have 2 tests left. Make your next move.

Assuming the machine lights only when both nexioms are on it, the lit result means one nexiom is sudokes or gidimur, and the other is lireru or dizabir. That leaves 4 possible pairs, and 2 tests can separate 4 cases.

For this test I'll place sudokes with both lireru and dizabir. Since one of lireru and dizabir is definitely a nexiom, the machine will light exactly when sudokes is the other one. If it doesn't light, the nexiom from the first group is gidimur.

TEST: sudokes, lireru, dizabir
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have 1 test left. Make your next move.

Sudokes is not a nexiom, so the nexiom from the first group is gidimur. The other nexiom is lireru or dizabir. If I place gidimur with lireru, the machine will light only if lireru is the second nexiom. If it doesn't light, the second nexiom is dizabir.

TEST: gidimur, lireru
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have used all your tests. Give your ANSWER now.

Gidimur and lireru together did not light the machine, so lireru is not the second nexiom. That makes the pair **gidimur and dizabir**.

This depends on my working assumption that the machine lights only when both nexioms are on it. That rule fits all five results:
- **Test 1** (sudokes, gidimur, kigabe) held only gidimur, so it stayed dark.
- **Test 2** (lireru, dizabir, tefisi) held only dizabir, so it stayed dark.
- **Test 3** (sudokes, gidimur, lireru, dizabir) held both, so it lit.
- **Test 4** (sudokes, lireru, dizabir) held only dizabir, so it stayed dark.
- **Test 5** (gidimur, lireru) held only gidimur, so it stayed dark.

I didn't test the rule directly, so a stranger rule could give a different answer. But this pair is the one the simplest consistent explanation points to.

ANSWER: nexioms = gidimur, dizabir
One last question. If only dizabir were on the machine, with nothing else, would it light up? End your message with one line: PROBE: yes or PROBE: no

**No.** If gidimur and dizabir are the nexioms, then Test 2 (lireru, dizabir, tefisi) and Test 4 (sudokes, lireru, dizabir) each held dizabir plus only non-nexioms. Non-nexioms never affect the machine, so both tests behaved exactly as dizabir alone would, and neither lit up.

This conclusion relies less on my "both nexioms needed" assumption than the answer itself did. It only needs dizabir to be a nexiom and gidimur the other, so that neither test held a second nexiom. If dizabir turned out not to be a nexiom at all, it alone would be like an empty machine. That would almost certainly not light either.

PROBE: no
